title: New York Is Becoming the New Capital of Indian Fine Dining
excerpt: From a Michelin-starred tasting menu in Hudson Yards to a celebrity chef's debut in the East Village, a wave of ambitious Indian restaurants is reshaping how America eats.
body:
New York's Indian food scene is in the middle of an extraordinary moment. In just the past week, two high-profile Indian restaurants have opened — or are about to — in Manhattan, while London's beloved Dishoom edges closer to its first American outpost. For NRIs who grew up watching Indian food treated as an afterthought in the West, this is a turning point.

## A Michelin Star Moves East

On May 28, Indienne opens at Hudson Yards' Henry Hall, marking chef Sujan Sarkar's return to the city where he first made his name at Baar Baar in the East Village. The restaurant earned a Michelin star within its first year in Chicago's River North neighborhood and will bring its nine-course tasting menu format — priced at $195 for non-vegetarian and $175 for vegetarian and vegan — to a 34-seat space designed with Holi-inspired artwork and blush-toned interiors.

Sarkar is not stopping at one concept. He is simultaneously launching Apas, a high-end cocktail bar featuring South Asian botanicals, and Elder, a British-Indian chophouse that draws on the intertwined culinary histories of London and India. "Coming back with Indienne — and introducing two new concepts alongside it — feels like both a homecoming and a new beginning," Sarkar said.

## From Chopped Champion to Restaurant Owner

A week earlier, on May 21, celebrity chef Aarthi Sampath opened Drāvida at 211 1st Avenue. The Mumbai-born chef, who won Chopped and Beat Bobby Flay and trained at Michelin-starred Junoon, built her first restaurant around the idea of the South Asian diaspora's evolving palate. The menu reads like a map of migration itself: Lhasa Lamb Momo alongside Guyanese-style Doubles, Duck Nihari Hand Pie next to Oxtail Bunny Chow.

The two-floor East Village space, housed in a restored building with original brick ovens, also features Jam and Jaggery, a speakeasy in the basement. Drāvida is not just about Indian food — it is about everywhere Indian food has traveled.

## Dishoom's American Dream

Meanwhile, Dishoom — the London chain that turned Bombay's disappearing Irani cafés into a global phenomenon — is reportedly finalizing a site in New York for a late 2026 opening. Backed by private-equity firm L Catterton, the restaurant sold out a pop-up at Pastis last year and has been scouting locations in Manhattan. CEO Brian Trollip has confirmed he was recently in the city checking potential spaces.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For decades, the Indian dining experience in America was defined by a narrow band: buffet lunch specials, generic "curry houses," and the occasional high-end outlier. What is happening now is fundamentally different. These are Indian-origin chefs and entrepreneurs building restaurant empires on their own terms — tasting menus that start with chaat, cocktail bars named after Sanskrit words, and a London chain that treats a Bombay café with the reverence of a Parisian bistro.

The implications extend beyond New York. If Indienne, Drāvida, and Dishoom succeed — and the early signs suggest they will — they set a template for every major American city. Indian food is no longer seeking validation. It is setting the agenda.

## What's Next

The James Beard Foundation will announce its 2026 winners on June 15, and Indian-origin chefs and restaurants are among the finalists. The winners' ceremony in Chicago could add another chapter to what is already a landmark year for Indian cuisine in America. For the diaspora, the table has been set.
